abstract:
Lipid rafts (LRs) are relatively
well-ordered functional microdomains
in cell membranes and play an irreplaceable role in physiological
processes as a transduction platform for multiple signaling pathways.
Due to their small size and high spatiotemporal dynamics, it is difficult
to perform lipid raft-localized biomolecule imaging on the surface
of living cells. Here, we report a DNA nanotechnology-based platform
for reversible manipulation and localized analysis of lipid rafts,
which consists of two modules: “patching and coding probe pair”
and “fishing probe”. The probe pair is generated by
modifying two different sets of connectable DNA structures on a lipid
raft-specific protein. After recognizing lipid rafts, the two probes
in close proximity are linked by a DNA ligase reaction to form a lipid
raft identity (LR-ID) code. The LR-ID strand patches and stabilizes
the lipid raft structure. Interestingly, the raft patches formed can
be depatched by restriction endonucleases, providing the first reversible
manipulation of the lipid raft structure in living cells. We also
designed a “fishing probe” with a DNA hairpin structure
using an aptamer that can specifically bind to the target. The probe
can cascade the reaction to two input signals “LR-ID”
and “target protein” to generate an “off–on”
fluorescence switch, allowing imaging and dynamic monitoring of target
proteins localized in lipid rafts. By encoding arbitrary targets (in
the case of glycans) in lipid rafts, we have created a universal lipid
raft-localized imaging platform. This work provides an integrated
analytical and manipulative platform to reveal lipid rafts and associated
signaling pathways at the molecular level.

Introduction
Cell
membranes are composed of lipids and proteins and characterized
by horizontal heterogeneity.
1
,
2
In particular, there
are microdomains of specific lipids (e.g., cholesterol, saturated
sphingolipids) and proteins (e.g., glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored
proteins) assembled in a tightly ordered manner in the cell membrane,
called lipid rafts.
3
,
4
These microdomains can selectively
recruit specific proteins
4
such as mucin
1 (MUC1),
5
tyrosine kinase,
6
,
7
and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)
8
−
10
to trigger
signal transduction pathways by aggregating signaling molecules such
as membrane receptors or inducing structural modifications of specific
proteins.
11
These processes can mediate
a variety of cellular functions, including cellular endocytosis,
12
,
13
cell membrane sorting,
14
,
15
host–pathogen
interactions,
16
,
17
and immune signaling.
18
−
20
The recruitment of biomolecules to lipid rafts is regulated by several
factors,
4
including glycosylation.
21
−
23
McEver et al. found that
O
-glycosylation and terminal
sialylation were important for the targeting of P-selectin glycoprotein
ligand-1, CD43, and CD44 to lipid rafts.
22
Johnson et al. reported that decreased
N
-glycosylation
on neural cell adhesion molecule L1 (L1CAM) in the brain of CWH53
mutant mice reduced the proportion of L1CAM in lipid rafts, leading
to the development of hydrocephalus.
23
With a better understanding of cellular phase separation processes,
lipid rafts can be considered to be formed by phase separation driven
by lipid–lipid or lipid–protein interactions.
24
The localization of lipid rafts in situ on the
cell membrane, the analysis of lipid raft composition, and the tracking
of dynamic changes are the basis for exploring the mechanism of lipid
raft formation and its principles of action. However, lipid rafts
are dynamically changing, have no fixed boundaries, have lifetimes
ranging from milliseconds to minutes, and vary in size from 10 to
200 nm.
4
,
25
For example, substable lipid rafts of small
size can coalesce into relatively large and stable lipid rafts stimulated
by lipid–protein and protein–protein interactions.
24
These factors complicate lipid raft studies.
26
Cholera toxin B subunit (CTxB) is the
gold standard for in situ
labeling of lipid rafts.
27
It consists
of five peptide chains that are functionally similar to lectins and
specifically recognize monosialotetrahexosylganglioside (GM1)-enriched
lipid raft regions in a multivalent manner.
28
Although CTxB has a very strong affinity for GM1
29
(the
K
d
of monomeric CTxB binding
GM1 reaches 1.25 × 10
–8
M),
30
it enters cells very rapidly (<30 min) after binding.
31
,
32
Copatching is the most classical method for in situ visualization
of lipid raft molecules. The principle of the method is to use antibodies
to cross-link lipid raft-bound CTxB to patch lipid rafts and to confirm
the presence of target molecules on raft patches by immunofluorescence
colocalization after cell fixation.
22
,
33
This method
cannot follow the dynamic changes of a specific patch of lipid rafts,
and the signal is not strictly lipid raft specific at the molecular
level. In a previous study, our group used the recognition of lipid
rafts by CTxB to mediate the covalent labeling of the terminal galactose/
N
-acetylgalactosamine of the glycan chains in lipid rafts
to solve the problem of not being able to use CTxB to localize lipid
rafts on living cells for a long time.
31
However, this method is not universal for lipid raft biomolecules,
and there is a possibility of labeling nonraft glycans if the probe
size is larger than the lipid raft size. In terms of lipid raft manipulation,
some studies have used an aptamer that recognizes CTxB to cross-link
CTxB by inducing DNA assembly to enhance phase separation of the lipid
rafts from the nonraft region
34
or the
lipid raft marker, GPI-anchored protein placental alkaline phosphatase
(PLAP), to induce peptide self-assembly in lipid rafts to aggregate
the rafts.
35
,
36
However, these methods are either
limited by the unstable binding between CTxB and the aptamer or lack
lipid raft specificity at the molecular level and are difficult to
develop into lipid raft-specific detection methods.
Based on
the above considerations, we summarize the design principles
of the lipid raft molecule detection platform: (1) the aggregation
and stabilization of lipid rafts on living cells and the assembly
of the target-responsive analytical module in a lipid raft-localized
manner; (2) having a “lipid raft localization” →
“target response” → “signal reporting”
cascade signaling capability. Due to the programmable, modular design,
easy functionalization, and high biocompatibility of DNA,
37
−
39
herein, we developed a lipid raft-specific reversible manipulation,
component imaging, and dynamic monitoring platform by constructing
a DNA covalent binding network with CTxB as the node on living cells
and further combining it with dynamic DNA nanotechnology.
Results and Discussion
Design
Principle
The core of this platform is the design
of a “patching and coding probe pair” and a “fishing
probe” (
Scheme
1
). For the probe pair, we covalently modified CTxB with two different
sets of DNA fragments that can be ligated together (
Scheme
1
A), and the resulting probe
pair can specifically bind lipid rafts on living cells. When two different
probes are in close proximity, they can be linked by the action of
T4 DNA ligase.
40
The ligated DNA strand
stabilizes and patches the lipid rafts,
22
,
33
,
34
while its sequence represents the ID code for raft
regions (i.e., LR-ID). Patching and coding operations did not affect
cellular viability, and the CTxB-DNA cross-linked hybrid remained
stable on the cell membrane. In particular, unlike other lipid raft
manipulation strategies, the hybrid can be de-cross-linked using the
endonuclease AciI, allowing reversible manipulation of lipid rafts
on living cells. We also designed a hairpin-structured fishing probe
based on the aptamer sequence of the target protein
41
(
Scheme
1
B), which can respond to “LR-ID” and “target
protein” in a cascading manner.
42
The presence of the target protein in lipid rafts was indicated
by the fluorescence “off–on” switch.
43
We thus achieved the first dynamic visualization
of lipid raft proteins on living cells and further developed a universal
lipid raft biomolecule imaging platform to reveal the distribution
of lipid raft glycans in situ using sialic acids (Sia) as an example.
Scheme 1
Schematics of the Patching and Coding Platform for Lipid Raft-Localized
Imaging
(A) Schematic illustrating the
specific binding of the lipid raft (LR) probe pair (L1 and L2) to
cell surface lipid rafts and subsequent patching of the rafts using
T4 DNA ligase. L1 and L2 are CTxB-DNA hybrids with different DNA sequences
that, when linked by T4, can not only stabilize and assemble raft
patches but also provide an identification (LR-ID) code to indicate
lipid raft regions. (B) Scheme showing the principle of using the
fishing probe to perform lipid raft-specific biomolecule imaging.
Only when the fishing probe binds the LR-ID, can it recognize the
target, resulting in the restoration of fluorescence.
Investigation of the Feasibility of the DNA Ligation Reaction
Because lipid rafts are characterized by highly dynamic changes,
4
,
25
speed is a necessary requirement for lipid raft manipulation tools.
T4 DNA ligase (T4) can rapidly (within 30 min) and efficiently form
phosphodiester bonds between juxtaposed 5′-phosphate (P) and
3′-hydroxyl (OH) gaps in double-stranded DNA,
40
so we used this reaction to ligate DNA fragments. We designed
S1 (23 nt) and S2 (35 nt) sequences to construct a lipid raft probe
pair (
Table S1
) and a “glue sequence”
S* to assist T4: S* can hybridize stably with S2 (10 bp) and reversibly
and dynamically with S1 (6 bp). Upon S* hybridization to S2, T4 can
link the hydroxyl group at the 3′-end of S1 to phosphate at
the 5′-end of S2 to form an S chain (
Figure
1
A).

Design and fabrication of lipid raft probes.
(A) Scheme of the
DNA strand ligation reaction assisted by T4 DNA ligase (T4). (B) Native
PAGE analysis: mixture of S1 and S2 (lane 1), S* (lane 2), mixture
of S2 and S* after incubation at 37 °C for 1 h (lane 3), mixture
of S2·S* and S1 (lane 4), mixture of S and S* after incubation
at 37 °C for 1 h (lane 5), and mixture of S2·S*, S1, and

analysis of S1-Cy3, Cy5-S2·S*, and the mixture of both with or
without T4. Excitation wavelength: 543 nm. (D) UV–vis spectra
of CTxB, CTxB-S1, and S2-CTxB (2 μM in equivalent CTxB concentration).
(E) SDS-PAGE characterization of CTxB (lane 1), CTxB-SMCC (lane 2),
L1 (lane 3), S2-CTxB (lane 4), L2 (lane 5), the mixture of L1 and
L2 without (lane 6) and with (lane 7) T4 DNA ligase added, and T4
DNA ligase alone (lane 8). (F) MCF-7 cells were pretreated with 7KC
or PPMP to disrupt lipid rafts, followed by incubation with the mixture
of L1
S1-Cy3
and L2
S2-Cy5
and confocal
laser scanning microscope (CLSM) imaging. Scale bar: 10 μm.
Data are representative of three individual experiments.
We first used electrophoresis to verify the feasibility of
the
T4-mediated DNA ligation reaction in solution (
Figure
1
B). S2 was able to form a stably hybridized
double-stranded S2·S* with S* (lane 3). After mixing S2·S*
and S1 together, there was no change in the band of S2·S* (lane
4), while the S·S* band appeared at high molecular weight when
T4 ligase was added (lane 6), demonstrating that T4 can ligate S1
and S2 with the help of S* to generate S that could stably hybridize
with S*.
The ligation was further confirmed by the fluorescence
experiments
(
Figure
1
C). Cy5-modified
S2 (Cy5-S2) was incubated with S* and then mixed with Cy3-modified
S1 (S1-Cy3) and T4, and a clear fluorescence resonance energy transfer
(FRET) signal (659 nm, magenta line) could be observed, while no FRET
signal (black line) was observed without the addition of T4. The successful
ligation of S1 and S2·S* under the action of T4 lays the foundation
for the next step of constructing a cross-linkable lipid raft probe
pair.
Preparation of a Lipid Raft Probe Pair, and Verification of
the Cross-Linking Feasibility
We next prepared lipid raft
probes L1 and L2 by covalently modifying S1 and S2·S* on CTxB,
respectively. We first modified the amino group of CTxB with 4-(
N
-maleimidomethyl)cyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid 3-sulfo-
N
-hydroxysuccinimide ester sodium salt (SMCC) to produce
maleimidyl-modified CTxB (CTxB-SMCC)
44
and
then reacted with sulfhydryl-modified S1 (SH-S1) and S2 (S2-SH) to
produce CTxB-S1 (i.e., L1) and S2-CTxB, respectively (
Figure S1
). According to the MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry
data (
Figure S2
), 3–6 SMCCs were
attached to 1 CTxB monomer. CTxB-S1 and S2-CTxB showed distinct UV–vis
absorption peaks around 260 nm, confirming the successful attachment
of S1 (or S2) to CTxB (
Figure
1
D). From the absorption values, we deduced that each CTxB
pentamer was modified with an average of 3–4 S1 (or S2) chains.
We incubated S2-CTxB with S* to prepare the lipid raft probe L2 (S*·S2-CTxB).
We demonstrated the successful preparation of L1 and L2 and the
T4-assisted ligation of L1 and L2 by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide
gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) (
Figure
1
E). L1 (lane 3), S2-CTxB (lane 4), and L2 (lane 5)
all produced smeared bands that shifted upward relative to CTxB (lane
1). After addition of T4, a smeared band appeared at higher molecular
weights (lane 7), corresponding to the cross-linked lipid raft probes
(generating CTxB-DNA cross-linked hybrids).
DNA Ligation-Based Lipid
Raft Patching
To visualize
the recognition, cross-linking, and retention of the lipid raft probes
on the cell surface, we prepared two additional sets of fluorescently
labeled counterpart probes. (1) L
S
pair: Cy3 and Cy5 were
modified on S1 and S2 in L1 and L2, respectively, and the probes were
designated as L1
S1-Cy3
and L2
S2-Cy5
. (2) L
C
pair: Cy3 and Cy5 were attached to CTxB in L1
and L2, respectively, and the probes were designated as L1
C-Cy3
and L2
C-Cy5
. Using the human breast cancer cell
line MCF-7 as a model, the cells after incubation with L
S
showed a clear fluorescence on the cell membrane (
Figure S3
), similar to the fluorescence obtained with a commercially
available lipid raft imaging probe (CTxB-AF647), demonstrating the
ability of L
S
to bind to cells.
To confirm that L
S
was indeed bound to lipid rafts, we performed 7-ketocholesterol
(7KC)
45
and
dl
-threo-1-phenyl-2-palmitoylamino-3-morpholino-1-propanol
(PPMP)
46
lipid raft disruption experiments.
In the presence of methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD), 7KC replaces
cholesterol on the cell membrane, altering the lipid rafts from an
ordered state to a disordered (nonraft) state.
45
As expected, treatment of cells with 7KC supplemented with
MβCD reduced the binding signal of L
S
to background
fluorescence levels (
Figure
1
F). PPMP is able to block the synthesis of almost all sphingolipids,
including GM1, thereby inhibiting CTxB binding to cells.
46
Similarly, the binding signals of L
S
were significantly reduced after PPMP treatment (
Figure
1
F), demonstrating the recognition
specificity of the lipid raft probe pair to lipid rafts.
Next,
we cross-linked the lipid raft probe pair L
S
on
the surface of live cells using the T4 ligation reaction to patch
lipid rafts (
Figure
2
A). After the cells bound L
S
, a very weak FRET signal
appeared on the cell membrane (T4– group,
Figure
2
B). This is probably due to
the presence of six complementary bases between S1 and S2·S*,
which could generate a background FRET signal by reversible dynamic
hybridization.
47
The intensity of the FRET
signal between Cy3 and Cy5 increased after the addition of T4 (T4+
group). The FI
FRET
/FI
Cy3
ratio was calculated
by dividing the intensity of the FRET signal (FI
FRET
) by
the fluorescence intensity of Cy3 (FI
Cy3
),
34
and the ratio was found to increase compared to that without
T4 (
Figure S4A
). We also performed the
same experiment using the L
C
pair (
Figures
2
C and
S4B
). Since
in L
C
the fluorescence molecules were directly labeled
on the protein, the background FRET signal was significantly weaker
than when using the L
S
pair. The FI
FRET/
FI
Cy3
ratio became greater with increasing T4 incubation time,
peaking at 30 min and then declining slightly (
Figure S4D and S4E
).

We performed two sets of experiments to demonstrate
that the increase
in FRET signal is dependent on the DNA ligation reaction. (1) We mixed
Cy3-modified and Cy5-modified CTxB (without DNA modification) with
cells and found only background FRET signal with or without addition
of T4 (
Figures
2
D and
S4C
). This experiment also demonstrated that
T4 ligase does not cause lipid raft patching. (2) We changed the partial
sequence of S* to construct the S′ strand, i.e., we replaced
six bases of S* that are complementary to S1 with noncomplementary
bases while leaving the S2-hybridization portion of S* unchanged.
The S′·S2 (Cy5)-CTxB was prepared by hybridizing S′
to S2-CTxB (S2 was modified with Cy5). We mixed this probe or S2 (Cy5)-CTxB
(without S*) with L1
S1-Cy3
, then added the mixture
to the cells, and initiated T4 ligation. In both cases, the FRET signal
was significantly reduced (
Figure S5
).
We also performed cross-linking with L
S
on 7KC or PPMP
pretreated cells. As expected, no FRET signal was generated in the
drug-treated groups (
Figure S6
). The above
results suggest that a robust covalent bond was formed between the
probe pair under the action of T4, thereby stabilizing and patching
the lipid raft structure through the strong binding between CTxB and
lipid rafts.
Depatching of Lipid Rafts
In contrast
to the antibody-based
22
,
33
or peptide self-assembly-based
lipid raft patching strategies,
35
,
36
our method enables
the cleavage of the DNA linkages between CTxB
nodes using restriction endonucleases, thereby realizing lipid raft
depatching in living cells (
Figure
2
E). We chose the endonuclease AciI, which can only
recognize double-stranded structures, to cleave S·S* (cleavage
site: S strand, 5′-ĈCGC-3′; S* strand, 5′-ĜCGG-3′).
48
We first verified that AciI can cleave S·S*
in solution by in-gel fluorescence experiments using L1 and L2
C-Cy5
: the band of the cross-linked hybrids at high
molecular weight disappeared (lane 5,
Figure
2
F). We then investigated the effect of AciI
treatment on FRET signals using the L
S
pair. A significant
decrease in FRET signal on the cell surface was observed after treatment
with AciI (200 U/mL) at 37 °C for 30 min (
Figures
2
G and
S7
), indicating
that the DNA linkages between the Ls pair were broken. This is the
first time that a reversible manipulation of lipid rafts on living
cells has been achieved and further demonstrates the ligation of L1
and L2 by T4.
Cytocompatibility of lipid raft patching is a
prerequisite for the next step of in situ imaging and dynamic tracking
of lipid raft components. We examined the effect of binding of probes
L1 and L2 to cells, followed by T4 treatment, on cellular viability
using the CCK-8 cell viability assay kit. Cellular viability was maintained
at ∼90% for both compared to untreated cells (
Figure S8
), indicating good cytocompatibility of the DNA ligation-based
lipid raft patching operation. Due to the effect of the AciI buffer
system on the cells, the cellular viability was reduced after the
depatching operation but maintained at 65%, which could be overcome
by optimizing the buffer solution.
Verification of the Patching
and Depatching of Lipid Rafts
Having fully confirmed the
cross-linking and de-cross-linking of
the probe pair on cells, we next demonstrated that these manipulations
cause lipid rafts to undergo patching and depatching. Flotillin-1,
one of the major markers of lipid rafts,
49
is highly correlated with poor cancer prognosis.
50
We investigated the distribution of flotillin-1 on cell
membranes after different manipulations to confirm that the rafts
were indeed regulated. Immunofluorescence was performed using super-resolution
microscopy equipped with a stimulated emission depletion (STED)
51
module (
Figure
3
A). Before probe cross-linking (unpatched group) and
after de-cross-linking (depatched group), the distribution of flotillin-1
on the cell membrane was similar to the untreated group, both in an
extremely fragmented form, and no clear cell membrane contours could
be seen, probably due to the small size of the unpatched lipid rafts
(10–200 nm); while for the patched group, the fluorescence
still showed a fragmented punctate distribution pattern, but the fragments
were larger and clearer, allowing the clear cell membrane contours
to be seen.
Figure 3
Demonstration of the patching and depatching of lipid rafts. (A)
Stimulated emission depletion (STED) images of the immunofluorescence
signal of flotillin-1 on MCF-7 cells before and after LR patching
and those after depatching treatment. The cells incubated only with
anti-flotillin-1 antibody were used as controls. Scale bars: 10 (top)
and 5 μm (bottom). (B–D) Fluorescence recovery after
photobleaching (FRAP) data of MCF-7 cells before and after LR patching
and those after depatching treatment. (B) CLSM images of the L1
C-Cy3
on MCF-7 cells at different recovery time points.
Scale bar: 5 μm. (C) Magnified CLSM images of cells 8 min after
photobleaching. Scale bar: 1 μm. (D) Plots of fluorescence recovery
percentage in the region of interest shown in B versus time. Images
are representative of three individual experiments.
Next, we performed a fluorescence recovery after photobleaching
(FRAP)
34
assay to confirm the patching
and depatching of lipid rafts (
Figure
3
B–D). After mounting the L
C
pair
on the cell surface, we chose Cy3 labeled on L1
C-Cy3
as the bleaching target. After bleaching a selected circular area
with a strong laser, the Cy3 fluorescence signal in this area disappeared.
We collected the fluorescence recovery signal of the selected region
of the cell membrane in the unpatched, patched, and depatched groups
at different time points. After 6 min of recovery, the fluorescence
of the unpatched and depatched groups recovered to 30% and 17%, respectively,
while the patched group was basically not recovered. With the extension
of the recovery time to about 8 min, the fluorescence recovery signals
of all three cell groups increased and the fluorescence recovered
to about 40% and 30% in the unpatched and depatched groups, respectively,
while the signal of the patched group remained at a lower level of
13.6%, and the trend of fluorescence recovery was significantly slower
than that of the other two cell groups.
Based on these phenomena,
we speculate that the covalent DNA network
formed by the probes strongly anchored in lipid rafts stabilizes and
patches the underlying lipid rafts and enhances the phase separation
between the lipid raft and the nonraft regions, which eventually leads
to slower cell membrane flow and lower fluorescence signal recovery.
34
In the unpatched group, the cell membrane flow
was relatively faster; similarly, when the covalent linkages between
the probes were broken after AciI digestion, the restriction on cell
membrane flow was released and the fluorescence recovery was correspondingly
faster. In addition, the fluorescence recovery rate of the depatched
group was intermediate between that of the unpatched and patched groups,
which may be due to the longer time required for the patched lipid
rafts to return to the undisturbed state. These phenomena strongly
confirm that our method indeed enables the manipulation of the distribution
of lipid rafts on living cells. Since lipid rafts play an important
role in cell adhesion and polarization, we predict that lipid raft
patching could affect cell adhesion behaviors as well as signaling
pathways associated with cell surface adhesion proteins (noting that
due to the formation of the DNA-CTxB conjugate network, the biomolecular
composition of rafts may not be susceptible to change). Thus, the
proposed lipid raft manipulation method is a promising tool to gain
insight into lipid raft functions.
Investigation of the Retention
Time of the Cross-Linked CTxB-DNA
Hybrids on the Surface of Living Cells
Although CTxB is the
gold standard for lipid raft labeling, it is rapidly internalized
by cells through mechanisms such as inducing glycolipid aggregation,
causing changes in cell membrane curvature, and activating the endocytosis
pathway
27
,
28
(most has entered the cell after 30–60
min at 37 °C), making it difficult to use CTxB for prolonged
localization and manipulation of lipid rafts. In this regard, we examined
the retention time of L
C
on the cell membrane with or without
DNA ligation and compared it with that of commercial CTxB-AF647 (
Figure S9A
).
After incubation of either
L
C
or CTxB-AF647 with cells in an ice–water bath
for 30 min, a clear fluorescent signal appeared on the surface of
the cell membrane (
Figure S9B and S9C
).
Since the T4 reaction needs to be performed at 25 °C, the cells
bound with L
C
or CTxB-AF647 were then incubated at 25 °C
for 30 min (for the L
C
group, examined with or without
T4 addition) and then at 37 °C for different times (0–2
h). It was found that the fluorescence signal of the L
C
groups (T4+ and T4−) basically stayed on the cell membrane
within the observation time window, with little intracellular signal,
whereas the intracellular fluorescence signal of the T4+ group was
even lower, while the intracellular fluorescence signal of the CTxB-AF647
group was very strong after 1 h of incubation at 37 °C. These
data suggest that covalent modification of CTxB by DNA and DNA ligation
manipulation can significantly delay the internalization of CTxB,
allowing it to remain on the cell membrane for more than 2 h. This
provides the necessary conditions for the next step of localization
and dynamic tracking of lipid raft components using the CTxB-DNA cross-linked
hybrid.
Design Principle of the Lipid Raft-Specific Imaging Probe
The difficulty with lipid raft-specific imaging is how to target
the detection probe to the rafts. In our work, the DNA sequence of
the strand S formed by the lipid raft probe pair using T4 ligation
can be used as a lipid raft identity (LR-ID) code to indicate the
location of lipid rafts. To achieve imaging of target proteins in
lipid rafts, we designed a fishing probe that can specifically bind
to lipid rafts and then to target proteins through a two-step cascade
algorithm. (1) The fishing probe can only expose the domain that can
recognize the target molecule after recognizing the LR-ID (ensuring
lipid raft specificity); (2) the exposed domain can only undergo structural
changes after binding to the target molecule, allowing the signal
to switch on (ensuring protein specificity).
According to the
literature, MUC1 is often overexpressed in metastatic cancers and
is associated with increased tumor aggressiveness, metastatic ability,
and drug resistance and can be used as a diagnostic marker for the
metastatic process.
52
Lipid raft-localized
MUC1 can promote transendothelial metastasis of tumor cells by interacting
with other proteins, such as the intercellular adhesion molecule ICAM-1.
53
Therefore, we selected MUC1 on lipid rafts of
MCF-7 cells as a target protein and designed a fishing probe based
on the aptamer sequence S2.2,
41
which can
recognize MUC1 with high affinity and specificity. Aptamers are artificially
designed oligonucleotides that can specifically bind biological targets
through noncovalent interactions and have the advantages of customizability,
easy functionalization, high targeting, and low cytotoxicity; in particular,
they can be easily coupled to various DNA dynamic nanotechnologies.
54
The fishing probe we designed is a fluorophore
(FAM) and quencher
(Q) dual-modified DNA hairpin structure (FAM-H-Q) which consists of
two functional modules: (1)a LR-ID recognition–response module
(raft module, red and blue parts) and (2) a target recognition–response
module (target module, purple and gray parts) (
Figure
4
A). The raft module is located in the hairpin
stem and contains two domains, r1·r1* (blue) and r2* (red), where
r1* is blocked by r1 (8 bp) and is complementary to the r1 domain
of S (belonging to the original S1) and the r2* sequence (20 nt) is
complementary to the r2 domain of S (belonging to the original S2).
The target module consists of three domains: a, b*, and b. Domain
a (purple) is a truncated aptamer sequence (S2.2) of MUC1. Domains
b* and b (gray) are complementary. The fluorophore FAM and the quencher
Dabcyl are modified at the penultimate base at the 3′-end of
the r1* domain and the terminal base at the 3′-end of the b
domain, respectively, to ensure that the probe is fluorescently “off”.
The two modules have a “cascade response” capability.
42
When S·S* (Input 1, carrying LR-ID) is
present, r2*-r1* of the raft module replaces S* and hybridizes with
S,
47
unlocking the target module; the target
module can then respond to MUC1 (Input 2), generating a conformational
change and binding to MUC1. The stem-loop structure is fully opened,
and fluorescence is restored,
43
indicating
the presence of MUC1 in lipid rafts.

Next,
we validated the feasibility of the design. As a first step, the ability
of H to respond to LR-ID was investigated at both in-solution and
on-cell-surface levels. First, in electrophoresis experiments, after
incubating H with S, the bands of both strands became lighter and
the H·S band appeared (lane 5,
Figure
4

S. Both H·S and S* bands appeared after incubating H with prehybridized
S·S* (lane 6) or S·S* obtained from S1 and S2·S* (assisted
by T4 ligation) (lane 7), indicating that H can undergo a strand displacement
reaction with S·S* to release S* and obtain H·S.
Next,
we designed two sets of experiments on the surface of living cells
to investigate whether H can react with S·S*. We modified the
H probe with FAM at the 5′ end to yield FAM-H (
Figure S10A
). When L1 and L2 were not attached
to cells, FAM-H showed only a background adsorption signal on the
cell surface; when L1 and L2 were attached to the cell surface without
the addition of T4, a weak FAM fluorescence appeared on the cell surface.
This is due to the fact that H has 20 complementary bases with S2,
which is more than the number of complementary bases between S* and
S2 (10), so it can still replace S* and hybridize with S2. However,
at this time, the b*·b and r1*·r1 domains (14 bp in total)
of the hairpin stem of H are in the hybridized state and the target
module is still locked (see below for proof). When T4 was added to
cross-link L1 and L2, the cell surface binding of FAM-H increased
significantly. This is due to the fact that H hybridizes with S to
form a more stable double strand (28 bp), and the unhybridization
of r1* with r1 unlocks the target module, allowing domain a to bind
MUC1 in lipid rafts, thereby increasing the stability of FAM-H binding
to the cell surface.
We also hybridized the FAM-modified S*
chain (at the 3′
end, yielding S*-FAM) with S2-CTxB to produce L2
S*-FAM
, which was added to the cells along with L1, followed by T4 treatment,
to form S·S*-FAM. There was a clear fluorescence of S* on the
cell surface (
Figure S10B
); the fluorescence

was added to the system. This indicates that H can successfully replace

S2.2 (FAM-Apt), random sequence (FAM-Ran),

Dynamic
Tracking of Lipid Raft-Specific Proteins
We
then used the method to observe the dynamics of target molecules in
lipid rafts in real time. This has been a difficult problem for lipid
raft detection because of the lack of tools that can localize lipid
rafts for long periods of time. The CTxB-DNA cross-linked hybrids
that we assembled in lipid rafts of living cells could remain on the
cell membrane for long periods of time and can therefore interact
with the fishing probe at specified times as Input 1. We chose phorbol
12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA)-stimulated MCF-7 cells as a model. PMA
can enhance the cleavage of cell surface proteins and induce the release
of extracellular structural domains by activating protein kinase C
and other pathways.
56
The shedding of extracellular
structural domains of membrane proteins can release membrane-anchored
growth factors, convert membrane receptors into ligand competitors,
and unlock the function of cell adhesion receptors, which are important
pathways for regulating cell–extracellular interactions. After
patching and coding of lipid rafts, we treated the cells with PMA
for different periods of time, then added FAM-H-Q, and found that
the recovery of the fluorescence signal decreased with increasing
PMA treatment time (
Figure
4
H and
4
I). Since the binding of the
lipid raft probe pair to the cell surface was not affected by PMA
treatment (
Figure S14
), we confirmed that
the reduction in fluorescence signal after PMA treatment was due to
the shedding of the extracellular domain of MUC1. This experiment
demonstrates that our method can dynamically track changes in target
molecules in lipid rafts in situ.

Conclusion
We have developed a lipid raft-specific biomolecule imaging platform
that is applicable to living cells. The key to the platform is the
use of DNA strands as physical links to cross-link CTxB, which can
specifically recognize lipid rafts to enable lipid raft stabilization
and patching, and lipid raft-localized imaging in living cells. At
the same time, the DNA sequence information can be used as a lipid
raft identity (LR-ID) code to guide the positioning of the fishing
probe to lipid rafts. The fishing probe could only be switched on
after cascading the reaction to the LR-ID and the target molecule
(or DNA Tag on the target molecule), thus ensuring lipid raft and
target specificity. This not only provides a solution for imaging
arbitrary targets on lipid rafts but also represents a cross-dimensional
encoding concept that encodes both spatial microdomains and target
molecules. Taking advantage of the platform’s superior biocompatibility
and sufficient membrane residence time, we have achieved dynamic visualization
of biomolecules localized in lipid rafts. In particular, we have achieved
the first reversible manipulation of lipid rafts on the living cell
surface, providing a new perspective for in situ manipulation of lipid
rafts. Our method provides a powerful research tool to study the composition,
structure, and function of lipid rafts, contributing to the elucidation
of lipid raft-mediated cell–cell interactions, the regulatory
mechanisms of protein post-translational modifications on lipid raft
functions, and lipid raft-mediated signaling pathways associated with
disease pathogenesis. The strategy also has great potential for applications
in the screening of raft biomarkers and drug targets.
